column2: Five equal square tiles. How small a square box holds them all?
Four fit in a box two wide. The fifth has nowhere to go.
The obvious box is three wide, with room for four more.
Every tile lines up with the walls. Could turning one shrink the box?
Turn the middle tile. Its corners stay on a circle that only touches its neighbours, so nothing collides.
Now squeeze. The corner tiles slide in, and no two tiles ever overlap.
They stop when each inner corner touches the middle of a side of the turned tile.
Across the square gap, opposite inner corners are now one tile apart.
A square's diagonal is its side times the square root of two. So the gap is one over the square root of two, and the box is two plus that, about two point seven one.
Any further, and the corners bite in.
This shows five tiles fit. It can't show that nothing smaller fits. That needs a proof.
Why do straight tiles need a box three wide? Take a narrower box, and mark its floor a third and two thirds of the way along.
The marks cut the floor into three equal pieces, and each is shorter than one tile.
So a straight tile's shadow on the floor can't fit inside one piece. A mark always lands strictly inside it, away from its ends.
Mark the left wall the same way. Then every straight tile has one of these four pins strictly inside it.
Two tiles can't share a pin, because their insides never overlap. So how many straight tiles fit?
Four at most, one per pin. So five straight tiles need a box at least three wide.
At exactly three, each piece is a whole tile long. Tiles can then touch the marks with their edges only, and five fit.
But this only counts straight tiles. In the turned packing, no pin is inside the turned tile, so the pins can't rule out its smaller box.
